parole.significato: A belief that spirits inhabit some or all classes of natural objects or phenomena.
parole.testo: From anima + -ism, from Latin anima (“life", "breath", "soul”). Dated sense from German Animismus, coined c. 1720 by physicist/chemist Georg Ernst Stahl (1660-1734) See anima mundi.

parole.significato: A dipeptide compound present in birds and other vertebrates, originally isolated from goose muscle.
parole.testo: From Latin anser (“goose”) + -ine, after German Anserin.

parole.significato: A repository for holding things; a hiding place or relicary.
parole.testo: From Latin conditorium, from condere (“to hide”). See recondite and reconditory. The cake shop is from German Konditorei

From Latin docēns, present participle of doceō (“to teach”). In the meaning of a university grade, as used in some Central European countries, it is clipped version of private docent, privat-docent, from German Privatdozent, from German Dozent.

parole.significato: In Semitic languages, the “adjective degree of superiority”. In some languages such as Arabic, the concepts of comparat…
parole.testo: From Latin ēlātus (“exalted, lofty, high”) + -ive. Possibly borrowed from German, which has produced a great deal of pioneering Semitist literature, and where Elativ is a common term for absolute superlative in all languages.

parole.significato: Moment of theoretical suspension of all action.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin epocha or German Epoche, from Ancient Greek ἐποχή (epokhḗ). Doublet of epoch. This term was introduced by Husserl and other phenomenologists, although it also seems to be present in Aristotelian philosophy (as the concept did originate with Aristotle).

parole.significato: that which is; an entity, a being, an existent
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, coined by Ralph Manheim in his 1959 English translation of Martin Heidegger’s Einführung in die Metaphysik to render German Seiendes (as distinct from Sein) on the basis of *essens, a pseudo-Latin present participle of sum.

parole.significato: An organ or other body part that is or can be turned inside out, especially an anterior portion of some annelid worms c…
parole.testo: From New Latin intrōvertere, from intro- (“within”) and vertere (“to turn”). Popularized as a psychological term by the German works of Carl Jung. By surface analysis, intro- + -vert.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a pharaoh.
parole.testo: From Latin Pharaōn- (stem of Pharaō (“Pharaoh”)) + -ic, originally modelled on German pharaonisch.
From Latin praeferendum, modelled on German.
From Latin puella aeterna (“eternal girl”), female form of puer aeternus (“eternal boy”) (in Ovid, Metamorphoses), after use in German by CG Jung.

parole.significato: A child-god who is forever young.
parole.testo: From Latin puer aeternus (“eternal boy”) (in Ovid, Metamorphoses), after use in German by Carl Jung.

parole.significato: Various medieval and early modern coins or units of account
parole.testo: From Middle English solidus, from classical Latin solidus (“solid”), see below. Doublet of sol, sold, soldo, solid, sou, and xu. In numismatic and weight senses, via medieval Latin solidus (“various coins”), from Late Latin solidus (“a gold coin of the Roman Empire”). In chemical sense, via German S

parole.significato: Of, from, constituting, inhabiting, or pertaining to the Sudetes or the Sudetenland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Sūdēticus, but with pronunciation influenced by German Sudeten and sudetisch.

parole.significato: According to the rules of an old drinking game in which the drinker upturned the empty cup and had to drink more if the…
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism from super- + naculum, nagulum, Latinized form of German Nagel, intended to mean “upon the nail”, after the German phrase auf den Nagel (trinken).

parole.significato: A person who sometimes wears clothes traditionally worn by and associated with the opposite sex; typically a male who c…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin trāns + vestītus, form of vestiō (“to clothe, to dress”) (as in English vestment, vest). Literally, a "cross-dresser". From transvestitism, from German Transvestitismus, coined in 1910 by Magnus Hirschfeld (the practice itself is much older).
